purpose: Editorial planning index for General Fact-or-Cap. It reconciles published question identities and adds provisional topic, subtopic, question-type, and underlying-claim summaries to support coverage planning and human repetition review. It is not runtime content or a factual, source-support, rights, or publication approval record.

baselineSnapshot.validationBasis: npm run report:question-inventory on the snapshot; reports schema validity, IDs, and exact normalized prompt/completion matching only.

editorialDistribution.basis: Provisional editorial classifications in this ledger; counts are planning signals, not independently verified subject truth.

classificationConventions.basis: Classifications were assigned from the actual prompt and completion. Legacy category/tags/difficulty are retained only as context and did not determine the topic assignment.
classificationConventions.uncertainty: A null uncertaintyNote means no specific categorization concern was recorded during this baseline pass; all classifications remain provisional and may be revised by an editor.
classificationConventions.sourceStatus: Source name and URL are transcribed as supplied. not-assessed-by-this-ledger is not a finding that the claim is unsupported; it means the ledger did not inspect source passages. rightsOrReuse remains unknown.

editorialClassification.underlyingClaimSummary: The planet closest to the Sun is Mercury.
The largest planet in our solar system is Jupiter.
The hottest planet in our solar system is Venus.
The planet with the shortest day in the solar system is Jupiter.
A year on Mercury lasts about 88 Earth days.
Earth has one natural moon.
Mars has two moons, Phobos and Deimos.
Because the Moon rotates at the same rate it orbits Earth, the same lunar hemisphere always faces Earth.
The Moon moves away from Earth by about one inch each year.
Earth takes about 365.25 days to complete one orbit around the Sun.
Earth's yearly cycle of seasons is caused by the tilt of its axis.
The planet that rotates at a nearly right angle to its orbital plane, appearing to spin on its side, is Uranus.
The first planet discovered with the aid of a telescope was Uranus.
Neptune was discovered in 1846.
One orbit of Neptune around the Sun takes about 165 Earth years.
Saturn is the only planet in our solar system with an average density lower than water.
Saturn's rings are made mostly of chunks of ice and rock.
Iron minerals in Martian rocks and dust appear red because they have rusted.
The largest volcano in the solar system, Olympus Mons, is on Mars.
The planet that spins in the opposite direction from most planets is Venus.
The world's tallest mammals are giraffes.
A giraffe's tongue can be about 21 inches long.
The fastest land mammal is the cheetah.
The only mammals capable of true flight are bats.
Many bats use echolocation to locate objects in the dark.
The largest penguin species is the emperor penguin.
During incubation, a male emperor penguin keeps its egg warm on its feet.
A common octopus has eight arms.
The beak is the only hard part of an octopus's body.
When threatened, an octopus can release a cloud of ink to help it escape.
Along with echidnas, platypuses belong to the small group of mammals that lay eggs.
A male platypus can deliver venom with a sharp spur on a hind foot.
Although sometimes nicknamed a bear, the koala is a marsupial.
Koalas rely on eucalyptus trees for both food and habitat.
The largest land animals on Earth are African elephants.
An elephant's trunk contains about 40,000 muscles.
The largest animals known to have lived on Earth are blue whales.
Blue whales feed nearly exclusively on tiny shrimp-like animals called krill.
Beneath its fur, a polar bear has black skin.
The sea turtle species that lacks a hard, bony shell is the leatherback.
In seahorses, it is the male that carries the developing young in a brood pouch.
A seahorse can move its two eyes independently of each other.
The ocean covers more than 70 percent of Earth's surface.

editorialClassification.underlyingClaimSummary: The Equator lies at 0 degrees latitude.
The Equator divides Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.
Earth's circumference at the Equator is about 40,075 kilometers.
Earth's equatorial bulge is caused by the planet's rotation.
At the Equator, Earth's surface spins at about 1,670 kilometers per hour.
Apollo 11 launched on July 16, 1969.
Apollo 11's lunar module landed in the Moon's Sea of Tranquility.
The two Apollo 11 astronauts who descended to the lunar surface were Neil Armstrong and Edwin “Buzz” Aldrin.
The Apollo 11 astronaut who piloted the command module while Armstrong and Aldrin were on the Moon was Michael Collins.
NASA estimated that about 650 million people watched Armstrong's televised Apollo 11 image.
Around 3100 B.C., a king united Upper and Lower Egypt.
Ancient Egyptians used hieroglyphic writing for records such as royal decrees and taxes.
The Nile River flows from south to north.
The Old Kingdom of Egypt is sometimes called the “Age of the Pyramids.”.
The Yayoi people in Japan began growing rice in flooded paddy fields.
In the 12th century, military rulers called shoguns took control of Japan.
Japan's 17th-century isolation from foreigners lasted more than 200 years.
In 1868 the shoguns were overthrown and emperors returned to power in Japan.
In ancient Greece, Athens, Sparta, Thebes, and Corinth were examples of city-states.
According to National Geographic Kids, Athens instituted a system of democracy in 508 B.C.
The ancient Olympic Games were held in the Greek city of Olympia.
The Olympic Games began again in Athens in 1896.
The first Chinese empire began under the Qin dynasty in 221 B.C.
Among the inventions credited to ancient China are paper, printing, silk, gunpowder, and the magnetic compass.
The Suez Canal links the Mediterranean Sea with the Red Sea.
Ocean tides respond to forces exerted by the Moon and the Sun.

sourceReview.sourceName: NOAA Ocean Service — Introduction to Tides

editorialClassification.underlyingClaimSummary: A geyser differs from an ordinary hot spring because its plumbing contains one or more constrictions that restrict water flow.

Apollo astronauts left a special mirror on the Moon so scientists could measure the Earth-Moon distance with laser light.

An octopus has three hearts, and its blood is blue.

repetitionReviewClusters.note: Multiple familiar solar-system facts include several size/extreme-property, orbital, and rotation formats. The claims are not asserted to be duplicates; review future batches for overconcentration and compare underlying facts.

Related ocean/water quantities and salinity-source facts share subject matter and some cited source pages. Claims differ by measurement or mechanism; use the cluster to avoid repetitive batch composition.
Several distinct geographic and geophysical facts use the Equator as context. Review for subject concentration; not a duplicate determination.
A concentrated set of Apollo/spaceflight history questions. Underlying claims differ, but future batches should avoid extending the same mission cluster without editorial justification.
Four distinct anatomical/defense facts about octopuses occur across two packs. Not exact or asserted semantic duplicates; review for repeated subject and biology-fact style.
